lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on taming rising prices
lead.head: How India learnt to love a target

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 68

body: Amit Varma started with ap­ples. If mag­gots ruin the or­chard that feeds a town, he said, ap­ples get dearer. That is sup­ply and de­mand, not in­fla­tion, which is when nearly ev­ery­thing goes up at once.

It hap­pens, he said, when the quan­tity of money changes and the goods and ser­vices stay the same. “Milton Friedman once fa­mously said in­fla­tion is al­ways and ev­ery­where a mon­e­tary phe­nom­e­non,” Varma said. {068-C01}
Because the new money is not shared out in pro­por­tion to what peo­ple al­ready have, the poor suf­fer most. “Inflation is a tax on the poor,” Varma said. {068-C02}

From there Ajay Shah, who was part of the pol­icy com­mu­nity that made in­fla­tion tar­get­ing hap­pen in India, took over. His case was that low and sta­ble in­fla­tion mat­ters far more than it seems, and that India fi­nally got the ma­chin­ery for it right.
## The hid­den costs
Inflation is not the price of growth, Shah ar­gued. It gets in the way of growth, in three ways.

First, it scram­bles sig­nals. Firms read a chang­ing world through prices. When ap­ples get dearer, a firm can­not tell whether they are scarce, wanted more, or sim­ply caught up in in­fla­tion. “The deep in­sight is that high in­fla­tion messes with the in­for­ma­tion pro­cess­ing prob­lem of firms,” he said. {068-C05}

Second, it eats con­tracts. Firms bind them­selves to one an­other through deals writ­ten in ru­pees, and in­fla­tion forces them to rene­go­ti­ate though noth­ing real has changed. That burns the ef­fort they need for real change. {068-C06}

Third, it short­ens sight. “In an en­vi­ron­ment with high and vari­able in­fla­tion, the fu­ture gets re­duced into the present,” Shah said. {068-C07} People stop plan­ning be­yond a cou­ple of years, and the long projects that bring growth suf­fer.
Growth, Varma added, is “the great­est god”, be­cause only growth gets a na­tion out of poverty. {068-C08}
## A tar­get with teeth
Chasing any­thing else, Shah said, al­ways comes at the cost of one task. “The core dharma of a cen­tral bank is to de­liver low and sta­ble in­fla­tion.” {068-C09}

The way to hold it to that job came from New Zealand in 1987: an in­fla­tion tar­get writ­ten into law by par­lia­ment, which grants the cen­tral bank its power over money. New Zealand even paid se­nior cen­tral bank staff a bonus for hit­ting it. {#nz1987}
Today, Shah said, all the ad­vanced economies tar­get in­fla­tion, though “some of them are too po­lite or too cheap to offer a bonus”.
## India’s way
In India, Shah was dis­cussing in­fla­tion tar­get­ing with Yashwant Sinha as early as 2002. {068-S04}
The 2007 boom, when the RBI bought dol­lars to hold down the rupee and flooded the econ­omy with money, ended in an in­fla­tion cri­sis that won the ar­gu­ment among econ­o­mists. {068-S05}
When the draft law stalled, Shah and KP Krishnan bor­rowed a 1990s trick: a signed agree­ment be­tween the fi­nance min­istry and the RBI. {068-S07}

P. Chidambaram left the de­ci­sion to his suc­ces­sor; Arun Jaitley said yes overnight. The agree­ment was signed on 20 February 2015, and in 2016 the RBI Act was amended to make in­fla­tion tar­get­ing law.
The amend­ment struck out the words that had de­scribed the RBI since 1934: “as a tem­po­rary mea­sure”. {068-S10}
Varma’s part­ing ad­vice was never to nor­malise any­thing or take the world for granted. “We’ve got to pre­serve the lit­tle good that we have done in the world,” he said. {068-R01}

second.label: The RBI Act
second.head: The stopgap that grew up
second.deck: In 2016, the RBI Act finally said what the central bank is for

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the RBI’s temporary preamble

body: When the British cre­ated the Reserve Bank of India in 1934, Ajay Shah said, “they cor­rectly un­der­stood that they don’t un­der­stand”. {#rbi1934} The pre­am­ble said the in­ter­na­tional mon­e­tary sys­tem was too dis­or­gan­ised to set­tle India’s mon­e­tary ar­range­ments.

So the bank was cre­ated “as a tem­po­rary mea­sure”. The words sur­vived until 2016, when the amend­ment that wrote in­fla­tion tar­get­ing into the RBI Act re­placed them with “in order to de­liver price sta­bil­ity”. {068-S10}
Shah rel­ished the change. His one re­gret was that the agree­ment be­hind it, signed on 20 February 2015 by Rajiv Mehrishi and Raghuram Rajan, was not done as a pub­lic show. {#feb2015}

quote.text: on his fore­head was the word, you’re a tem­po­rary mea­sure, be­cause we haven’t yet fig­ured out what to do.

third.head: A house for a loaf
body: Germany after the First World War, Amit Varma said, is a great ex­am­ple of hy­per­in­fla­tion. The win­ning na­tions de­manded repa­ra­tions so high that Germany had no op­tion but to print tons of money.
Prices went com­pletely out of whack: what could buy a house one week, Varma said, bought a loaf of bread the next. The chaos fed the right-wing ex­trem­ism that pro­duced Adolf Hitler.

John Maynard Keynes wrote about it at the time in *The Economic Consequences of the Peace*. {068-R03} One rea­son for such crazy de­mands, Keynes pointed out, was that no­body knew na­tional wealth. {068-S01}
That gap, Varma said, cre­ated the de­mand for some­thing like GDP, which did not then exist. “That’s a whole dif­fer­ent story,” he added, point­ing lis­ten­ers to his own episode on GDP.

box.title: Friedman’s long shadow
box.text: Amit Varma opened with Milton Friedman’s fa­mous line that in­fla­tion is al­ways and ev­ery­where a mon­e­tary phe­nom­e­non. Ajay Shah traced the deeper in­sight, that in­fla­tion scram­bles the price sig­nals firms rely on, to Friedman’s 1968 paper, *The Role of Monetary Policy*. {#friedman1968}

sections.label: The basics
sections.head: Too much money, too few goods
sections.caption: inflation as a tax on the poor
body: Amit Varma set out to ex­plain in­fla­tion in the sim­plest terms, a “re­ally dumbed down, sim­plis­tic ver­sion”, for any­one who had never thought about it be­fore.

Prices are set by sup­ply and de­mand. If mag­gots ruin the or­chard that grows a town’s ap­ples, ap­ples get dearer. That is not in­fla­tion. Inflation is when toma­toes, onions and mo­bile phones all go up to­gether.

Picture money on one side and goods and ser­vices on the other, he said, held in bal­ance by prices. If the gov­ern­ment prints twenty per cent more money and the goods stay the same, ev­ery­thing costs more. {#twenty}
## Who pays the bill

The state has a mo­nop­oly on money. A gov­ern­ment can print it to fund pop­u­lar schemes, and ev­ery­one says the gov­ern­ment is doing so much: it works po­lit­i­cally. But prices rise for ev­ery­one, and the new money is not shared in pro­por­tion to what peo­ple al­ready have. {068-C02}
So the poor suf­fer most, Varma said. “If there is ram­pant in­fla­tion, you have to hold your gov­ern­ment ac­count­able.”
Varma leaned on Milton Friedman’s fa­mous line that in­fla­tion is al­ways and ev­ery­where a mon­e­tary phe­nom­e­non. {068-C01}

~ Governments no longer lit­er­ally print money, he noted. The cen­tral bank, which holds the mo­nop­oly, can steer the money sup­ply through in­ter­est rates, so in­fla­tion is di­rectly in its con­trol.

quote.text: in­evitably the poor are the great­est suf­fer­ers, which is why I keep re­mind­ing peo­ple, in­fla­tion is a tax on the poor.

sections.label: The measure
sections.head: Bacon, bread and the basket
sections.caption: how inflation is measured
body: Start with your own shop­ping, Ajay Shah said. Multiply the quan­tity of each thing you buy by its price, add it all up, and do it again next month with new prices.
For Amit Varma, a “good de­vout non veg­e­tar­ian”, that means vast amounts of bacon and tiny amounts of bread. {#bacon}
Some prices rise and some fall, and on av­er­age that noise can­cels out. “The av­er­age over­all sys­tem­atic in­crease in the cost of your bas­ket is your in­fla­tion,” Shah said. {068-C03}
## The na­tional bas­ket

Statisticians do the same for the whole coun­try. Vast house­hold sur­veys sup­ply the weights: the CMIE sur­vey cov­ers about 190,000 house­holds three times a year, ask­ing about some 90 items. {068-R11} The weights stay fixed for a cou­ple of years, and each month’s prices are plugged in.
The re­sult, the con­sumer price index, matches nobody’s life ex­actly, but it re­flects the av­er­age house­hold.
Shah is scep­ti­cal of gov­ern­ment data by de­fault. But when he and Ila Patnaik cross-checked the CPI’s weights and prices against in­de­pen­dent sources, both broadly held up. {068-S02}
~ The Wholesale Price Index is an­other mat­ter, he warned. It has noth­ing whole­sale about it and re­flects nobody’s bas­ket. “What human being eats nickel?” {068-J03}

quote.text: Use the CPI. CPI is a de­cent good index and it is mean­ing­ful.

sections.label: The costs
sections.head: Static on the dashboard
sections.caption: why inflation matters
body: Is a point or two of in­fla­tion re­ally a prob­lem? Ajay Shah began with the price sys­tem, and a world that, as in “ei­ther Hindu or Buddhist phi­los­o­phy”, is ever chang­ing. {068-J07}

Tastes and tech­nol­ogy shift, and firms read those shifts through prices and adapt. “In the use of knowl­edge in so­ci­ety, the heavy lift­ing is being done by prices,” Shah said, echo­ing Friedrich Hayek’s essay. “Now don’t put noise into prices.” {068-R06}

Inflation does ex­actly that. A firm see­ing dearer ap­ples can­not tell if ap­ples are scarce or prices are sim­ply ris­ing, and high in­fla­tion is also vari­able in­fla­tion. Firms are mis­led into wrong ad­just­ments. {068-C05}
## Muscle and acid

Adjusting is ex­haust­ing, and every firm has a fi­nite bud­get of what Shah called ad­just­ment mus­cle. Inflation forces firms to rene­go­ti­ate con­tracts writ­ten in ru­pees, though noth­ing real has changed.

Shah’s ex­am­ple was a con­tract pay­ing Amit Varma ten lakh ru­pees an episode “to the great pod­caster”. Varma as­sured lis­ten­ers that the hosts are paid noth­ing: “It’s a labour of love.” {068-J04} After nine per cent in­fla­tion, Shah imag­ined Varma grum­bling that “Mr BeerBiceps” is paid much bet­ter.
~ The third cost falls on the fu­ture. With high and vari­able in­fla­tion, Shah said, “your plan­ning hori­zon shrinks”, and the long, com­plex projects that bring growth go un­built. {068-C07}

quote.text: high and vari­able in­fla­tion is the acid that drips on these con­tracts and de­stroys their mean­ing.

sections.label: The target
sections.head: Power, meet accountability
sections.caption: making central banks accountable
body: Parliament gives the cen­tral bank the power to cre­ate fiat money, Ajay Shah said, and a basic rule of pub­lic ad­min­is­tra­tion is that every grant of power comes with checks. {068-C10}
Being ap­pointed to run a cen­tral bank does not make any­one a good guy. That, he said, is sim­ple pub­lic choice the­ory.

Central banks have a long his­tory of fail­ure. The fix came from New Zealand in 1987: an in­fla­tion tar­get writ­ten into law, with a bonus for se­nior staff who hit it. {#nz1987} Parliament is the prin­ci­pal; the cen­tral bank is its agent.

Shah re­called Keynes wish­ing that econ­o­mists would be hum­ble like den­tists, a line that, he said, al­ways gets ap­plied to cen­tral bankers. {068-J08} Treat the cen­tral bank like a den­tist, he said: do the root canal well, and you get a bonus.
## Between two ex­tremes
Amit Varma called the tar­get el­e­gant. A cen­tral bank run by the gov­ern­ment would do pop­ulist things; one left to do what­ever it wants could be cap­tured by spe­cial in­ter­ests.

Shah spelt out both dan­gers. Government con­trol brings an elec­tion busi­ness cycle. At the other ex­treme are econ­o­mists who think pub­lic choice the­ory ap­plies to ev­ery­one but them­selves. {068-C11}
~ The tar­get sits be­tween the two, Varma said: de­fine one job, stay out of the way, and hold the bank to ac­count if it misses.

quote.text: But for us, we’re good guys and we should be given a free hand and we should do what­ever we want.

sections.label: The boiler room
sections.head: One lever, slow steering
sections.caption: the central bank’s single lever
body: Good cen­tral banks, Ajay Shah said, tin­ker with only one price: the short-term in­ter­est rate. Long-term rates, the ex­change rate and eq­uity prices are left to the mar­ket. “In all mod­ern cen­tral banks, we are all Wicksellian now.” {068-J10}
The dif­fi­culty is the lag. A rate change works on in­fla­tion slowly, like a car that re­sponds long after you turn the wheel, so a cen­tral bank has to fore­cast rather than react. {068-C12}
In India, Shah ad­mit­ted, the mod­els are abysmal, so the cen­tral bank may have lit­tle choice but to re­spond to the present.
## Brakes and ac­cel­er­a­tor
In a boom, in­fla­tion tends to rise and the cen­tral bank raises rates. Home loans, car loans and cor­po­rate debt get dearer, and the econ­omy cools. It is meant to watch in­fla­tion, not the boom.

In a cri­sis it cuts. The day India an­nounced the world’s most ex­ten­sive COVID lock­down, Shah said, no­body needed a model to see trou­ble ahead, and the RBI rightly brought rates down fast. {#covid}
~ The booms Shah had in mind were 1997 and 2007. Young lis­ten­ers who missed them, he lamented, “have no idea what eco­nomic suc­cess looks like”. {068-J13}

quote.text: In the en­gine room, there’s only one joy­stick where you’re con­trol­ling the short term rate. It’s one scalar, so not even a joy­stick.

sections.label: The India story
sections.head: A band, not a bullseye
sections.caption: India’s target and the old RBI
body: Why 4 per cent, when ad­vanced economies aim for 2? Zero is out, Amit Varma noted, for fear of de­fla­tion. But 2, Ajay Shah said, is per­ilously close to zero, and a cen­tral bank can­not use­fully cut rates below it.

India also has a deeply bro­ken fi­nan­cial sys­tem that muf­fles rate changes. Where a so­phis­ti­cated sys­tem needs a 25 or 50 basis point move, India needs big­ger ones, and so more head­room. {#basis}
Weak trans­mis­sion rules out pre­ci­sion too. “It is an un­rea­son­able task to ask the cen­tral bank that get me pre­cisely 4.00,” Shah said. Hence a band of 2 to 6 per cent. {068-C13}
Two quar­ters out­side the band oblige the RBI to ex­plain in pub­lic what went wrong. Varma rel­ished hear­ing “cen­tral banker” and “pen­i­tent” in the same sen­tence. {068-J12}
## The old RBI
Getting there took years. In the bad old days, Shah said, the RBI was not a real cen­tral bank but a cen­tral plan­ning agency, a hand­maiden of the gov­ern­ment. {068-S03}
C. Rangarajan and deputy gov­er­nor Tarapore rethought it in the 1990s. Then the RBI slid into a long so­cial­ist pe­riod, and the think­ing moved to academia and the Ministry of Finance.
~ Shah summed up that period’s at­ti­tude with Montagu Norman, the for­mer Bank of England gov­er­nor: “I don’t have rea­sons, I have my in­stincts.” {068-J09}

quote.text: Like re­ally, when you look at it, it was just an awful cen­tral plan­ning or­ga­ni­za­tion with lit­tle by way of re­deem­ing fea­tures.
We achieved some­thing beau­ti­ful called in­fla­tion tar­get­ing. It took a while, we got there. It is one rare, el­e­gant piece of great leg­is­la­tion, but these things are al­ways under threat.

p3.title: Inside the reform
p3.deck: Four tales of how inflation targeting won its long argument in India

stories.kicker: Amit Varma retells a story from his KP Krishnan episode
stories.head: Who am I to argue?
body: By the end of 2013 or early 2014, as Ajay Shah re­mem­bered it, a draft Monetary Policy Framework Agreement sat with the fi­nance min­is­ter, P. Chidambaram. It had been worked over by KP Krishnan and Chidambaram, and dis­cussed with Montek Ahluwalia and Manmohan Singh.

Chidambaram wrote on the file that it was one of the most im­por­tant mile­stones in the his­tory of India. But it should not be the work of a lame-duck gov­ern­ment, he wrote, and he left it to his suc­ces­sor, cor­rectly pre­dict­ing that it would not be him. {068-S08}
The suc­ces­sor was Arun Jaitley. Amit Varma re­told what hap­pened next as Krishnan had told it to him, in an episode Varma called an “eight hour mas­ter­piece”. {#eighthour}
Krishnan handed the new min­is­ter the file, per­haps on the evening of the same day, and told him it was re­ally big. The next morn­ing Jaitley called: yes, let’s do it.
Krishnan was alarmed. He wanted it done, but this was far-reaching. It changed ev­ery­thing. Had the min­is­ter ac­tu­ally read it?

Jaitley, a lit­tle ir­ri­tated, said he had gone through it. Then he made his point: “If this country’s finest eco­nomic mind and finest legal mind have said that this must be done, then who am I to argue?” He meant Manmohan Singh and P. Chidambaram. {068-S09}

~ For Varma this was grace across party lines, and it was also an end­ing. “This never hap­pens again,” he said. Politics, in his telling, changed for­ever, and today on every side of the aisle there is “just a dif­fer­ent class of peo­ple”.
stories.why: Years of re­form work cleared their last hur­dle be­cause one politi­cian de­ferred to his opponents’ ex­per­tise. Trust across party lines, the story sug­gests, is a kind of in­sti­tu­tional cap­i­tal, and it can dis­ap­pear qui­etly.
stories.postscript: In 2016 the RBI Act was amended to build in in­fla­tion tar­get­ing and a mon­e­tary pol­icy com­mit­tee.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Arun Jaitley’s overnight yes

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a reform that had to wait its turn
stories.head: Too early, said the minister
body: In 2002, years be­fore the idea be­came law, Ajay Shah was al­ready talk­ing to Yashwant Sinha about in­fla­tion tar­get­ing. {068-S04}

These ideas, Sinha said, were way ahead of any­thing India’s in­tel­li­gentsia was dis­cussing. They would need to be­come much more nor­mal in Indian in­tel­lec­tual de­bate be­fore some fu­ture fi­nance min­is­ter could act on them.
Shah ac­cepted the point. “Point well taken,” he said, look­ing back. “This is the way it should be done.”

~ The RBI of the day, Shah said, wanted de­tailed con­trol of the fi­nan­cial sys­tem and the ex­change rate, and no ac­count­abil­ity for in­fla­tion. Until the ar­gu­ment was won, the think­ing lived in academia and the Ministry of Finance.
stories.why: A re­form must win the ar­gu­ment in pub­lic de­bate long be­fore it can win in gov­ern­ment. That jour­ney through the pipe­line, Amit Varma said, is the sub­ject of the hosts’ episode *The Long Road to Change*. {068-R09}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the 2002 talk with Yashwant Sinha

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the boom that discredited the old RBI
stories.head: Buying dollars, printing trouble
body: In the go-go years of the mid-2000s, the econ­omy was boom­ing and for­eign cap­i­tal poured into India, as it does when times are good. The rupee ought to have risen.
Instead, Ajay Shah said, the RBI tried to fix the ex­change rate by buy­ing up the dol­lars, and it paid for them in ru­pees. {068-S05}
“And so the local econ­omy got flooded with ru­pees,” Shah said. “And so it was ex­pan­sion­ary mon­e­tary pol­icy at the worst pos­si­ble time. And that gen­er­ated a nice big in­fla­tion cri­sis.”
~ By and large, he said, that won the case among econ­o­mists. The old RBI could not just be ac­cepted in the mod­ern world; India needed to do bet­ter.
stories.why: A cen­tral bank that tries to steer the ex­change rate gives up con­trol of in­fla­tion. Pursue any other ob­jec­tive, Shah ar­gued ear­lier in the episode, and you will al­ways end up sac­ri­fic­ing the core one: low and sta­ble in­fla­tion. {068-C09}

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on borrowing a trick from the 1990s
stories.head: Four emails an hour
body: In 2013 the draft Indian Financial Code was stuck: P. Chidambaram said it was too big to pass so late in his government’s term. Ajay Shah, trav­el­ling abroad, and KP Krishnan traded “four emails per hour” on what to do. {#emails}

They re­mem­bered the 1990s, when Parliament could not pass a law to stop the RBI print­ing money for deficits. Instead the fi­nance min­istry and the RBI signed the Ways and Means Agreement, with Montek Ahluwalia and C. Rangarajan at a pub­lic cer­e­mony. {068-S07}
Shah and Krishnan pro­posed the same for in­fla­tion: a Monetary Policy Framework Agreement, in which the RBI would com­mit to a tar­get and the gov­ern­ment would not push it in other di­rec­tions.
~ Amit Varma sug­gested the first deal ben­e­fited from those two par­tic­u­lar peo­ple being in of­fice. A less en­light­ened RBI gov­er­nor, he said, might have pushed back.
stories.why: When the leg­isla­tive route is blocked, a pub­lic, signed com­mit­ment be­tween the two par­ties can de­liver the re­form first. The law, Shah noted, fol­lowed later, when the right time came.

quiz.q: Why, according to Amit Varma, does inflation hit the poor hardest?
quiz.a: New money isn’t shared out in pro­por­tion to what peo­ple al­ready have.

quiz.q: What three things did Ajay Shah say every reader must know about the Wholesale Price Index?
quiz.a: Nothing whole­sale about it, mean­ing­less as an index, but a use­ful price data­base.

quiz.q: Which country invented inflation targeting in 1987, and how did it reward central bankers?
quiz.a: New Zealand, which paid se­nior cen­tral bank staff a bonus for hit­ting it.

quiz.q: Why did India choose a 4 per cent target instead of the 2 per cent common elsewhere?
quiz.a: More room to cut rates in a slump, with a weak fi­nan­cial sys­tem.

quiz.q: What did the RBI do during the 2007 boom that set off an inflation crisis?
quiz.a: It bought dol­lars to stop the rupee ris­ing, flood­ing the econ­omy with ru­pees.

quiz.q: Which words did the 2016 amendment remove from the 1934 RBI Act’s preamble?
quiz.a: “As a tem­po­rary mea­sure”, re­placed with “in order to de­liver price sta­bil­ity”.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 68. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Arun Jaitley (Ministry of Defence, GODL-India); Milton Friedman (Bachrach Studios, public domain); Friedrich Hayek (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0); John Maynard Keynes (Wikimedia Commons, public domain).

shelf.title: Never normalize anything or take the world for granted
shelf.why: Inflation tar­get­ing is a rare, el­e­gant piece of good leg­is­la­tion, and gains like that are al­ways under threat.

shelf.title: Blue
shelf.creator: Joni Mitchell
shelf.why: Amit’s favourite Joni Mitchell album, by a singer-songwriter and gui­tarist ahead of her time whose polio-shaped gui­tar play­ing fits no sin­gle genre.

shelf.title: The Economic Consequences of the Peace
shelf.creator: John Maynard Keynes
shelf.why: Keynes’s vivid record of how glob­alised the pre-war world was and what war de­stroyed.

shelf.title: Demystifying GDP (Episode 130 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Rajeswari Sengupta
shelf.why: Rajeswari Sengupta on what GDP can and can­not mea­sure and how the num­ber is built, in­clud­ing how gov­ern­ment make-work and roads to nowhere in­flate it.

shelf.title: The Role of Monetary Policy
shelf.creator: Milton Friedman
shelf.why: The paper Ajay sees as the turn­ing point of 20th-century macro­eco­nomics in ideas and pol­icy: it treats peo­ple as op­ti­mis­ers, in­tro­duces the nat­u­ral rate of un­em­ploy­ment and con­fines mon­e­tary pol­icy to keep­ing prices sta­ble, be­cause in­fla­tion adds noise to price sig­nals.

shelf.title: The Use of Knowledge in Society
shelf.creator: Friedrich Hayek
shelf.why: Hayek’s ar­gu­ment that the knowl­edge needed to run an econ­omy is dis­persed among mil­lions of peo­ple, and that prices, not plan­ners, carry it: a lan­guage through which strangers tell each other what they want and lack.

shelf.title: Public Choice Theory Explains SO MUCH (Episode 33)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Explains that politi­cians and bu­reau­crats re­spond to in­cen­tives like ev­ery­one else, so the state is no benev­o­lent beast and gov­ern­ment fail­ure is far more com­mon than mar­ket fail­ure.

shelf.title: How to Do Development (Episode 57)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The case, built on Lant Pritchett’s ev­i­dence, that every human wel­fare in­di­ca­tor tracks per capita GDP, so sus­tained growth, not re­dis­tri­bu­tion or small solv­able projects, is the way out of poverty.

shelf.title: The Long Road to Change (Episode 36)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ the­ory of change: pol­icy im­proves through a decades-long pipe­line of data, re­search, rival pro­pos­als, pub­lic de­bate, com­mit­tee re­ports and draft laws, not by whis­per­ing in a joint secretary’s ear.

shelf.title: The Life and Times of KP Krishnan (Episode 355 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with KP Krishnan
shelf.why: An eight-hour oral his­tory from a re­former in­side the Indian state: how India han­dled the 2008 cri­sis, fought for in­fla­tion tar­get­ing and built the bank­ruptcy code.

shelf.title: CMIE Household Survey
shelf.creator: CMIE
shelf.why: CMIE’s house­hold sur­vey (about 190,000 house­holds, three times a year, across some 100 ho­mo­ge­neous re­gions) makes India’s di­ver­sity mea­sur­able, from five­fold in­come gaps be­tween re­gions to how many house­holds re­ally live off farm­ing.

shelf.title: Why is solving India’s inflation crisis important? (2012)
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s con­tem­po­rary ar­gu­ment for tack­ling in­fla­tion, writ­ten dur­ing the in­fla­tion cri­sis he de­scribes in this episode.

shelf.title: Designing the Monetary Policy Committee (2014)
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s de­sign for a mon­e­tary pol­icy com­mit­tee as a com­mit­ment de­vice: the gov­ern­ment-appointed gov­er­nor sits with four in­de­pen­dent econ­o­mists, so only one of five votes is ex­posed to po­lit­i­cal pres­sure.

shelf.title: Lost a shock absorber
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Further read­ing from Ajay along­side this episode on mon­e­tary pol­icy.

shelf.title: The Reformers (Episode 28)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The human story of the peo­ple who worked be­hind the scenes, often for decades and with­out re­ward, to open India up in 1991.

laughs.text: Ajay builds Amit’s per­sonal in­fla­tion bas­ket: ‘Vast amounts of bacon, tiny amounts of bread… Amit Bhai is a good de­vout non veg­e­tar­ian and he eats bacon as a mat­ter of prin­ci­ple.’ When the CMIE sur­vey comes up, Amit asks, ‘But no bacon?’ Ajay: ‘They have some generic cat­e­gories called meat and fish and so on, but not the sub­tlety of bacon.’

Ajay sug­gests a self-employed doc­tor can sim­ply charge more when prices rise. Amit: ‘Except some of your pa­tients die be­cause food is so ex­pen­sive they can’t af­ford it any­more, and then you have less pa­tients. I’m kid­ding.’ Ajay, al­ready reach­ing for the re­search on in­fla­tion shocks and in­fant mor­tal­ity: ‘Don’t even get me started.’
Ajay on the WPI’s nickel prices (‘what human being eats nickel’), and Amit’s sum­mary: ‘So the whole­sale price index is ba­si­cally not whole­sale, not an index, and not a price by it­self.’

Ajay’s hy­po­thet­i­cal con­tract pays ten lakh ru­pees per episode ‘to the great pod­caster.’ Amit tells view­ers, ‘we’re not get­ting any money for this. It’s a labor of love.’ Ajay then plays Amit rene­go­ti­at­ing after 9% in­fla­tion: ‘see Mr BeerBiceps, he gets paid so much bet­ter than me.’

After Ajay says a cen­tral bank must be ‘penitent’ when it misses its tar­get, Amit: ‘I love the way you use phrases cen­tral banker and pen­i­tent in the same sen­tence. You know, it re­minds me of the fa­mous song Please Forgive Me, No Matter What I Do.’

Ajay, half mock-epic and half rue­ful: ‘O ye young read­ers of Everything is Everything, if you haven’t lived in the glory years of 2007 and 1997, you have no idea what eco­nomic suc­cess looks like. You have just lived in some grim dark days and you have nor­mal­ized the sad­ness.’

Keynes on hu­mil­ity: Ajay first quotes it as cen­tral bankers being ‘hum­ble like den­tists,’ then cor­rects it to econ­o­mists, not­ing it al­ways gets ap­plied to cen­tral bankers. He ex­tends it: ‘we’ll treat you like a den­tist. If you did a root canal surgery and the tooth works out fine, then we’ll give you a bonus.’ On ad­vanced economies that skip New Zealand’s bonuses: ‘Some of them are too po­lite or too cheap to offer a bonus.’

Montagu Norman, the for­mer Bank of England gov­er­nor, quoted by Ajay as the model of an un­ac­count­able cen­tral banker: ‘I don’t have rea­sons, I have my in­stincts.’ Ajay then slips: ‘There should be a mys­tique of cen­tral plan­ning… Oh sorry, there should be a mys­tique of cen­tral bank­ing.’
‘In all mod­ern cen­tral banks, we are all Wicksellian now’: Ajay’s short­hand for cen­tral banks steer­ing by the short-term in­ter­est rate rather than by money sup­ply di­rectly.
